items.title: Full Opus 5 vs Kimi K3 vs GPT-5.6 vs Claude Fable 5 comparison.
items.summary:
Full Opus 5 vs Kimi K3 vs GPT-5.6 vs Claude Fable 5 comparison.

Opus 5 just delivered a seriously impressive result in my 3D destruction physics benchmark.

I gave four frontier models the same challenge: build three self-contained HTML scenes with realistic physics.

The tasks:

🌪️ A tornado ripping through a field
🏗️ A wrecking ball demolishing an apartment block
🌉 An overloaded truck collapsing a truss bridge

Token usage / cost:
• Opus 5: 55.9K tokens — $1.40
• Fable 5: 55.1K tokens — $2.82
• Kimi K3: 35.7K tokens — $0.55
• GPT-5.6: 20.1K tokens — $0.31

Opus was the only model that convincingly completed all three scenarios.

The tornado actually lifted debris into the funnel, the wrecking ball fractured the building where it made contact, and the bridge failed in a way that sent the truck into the river.

The others struggled in different ways. Fable’s tornado had little to pick up, its building collapsed before impact, and the bridge disintegrated unrealistically. GPT-5.6 was the cheapest, but the wrecking ball never reached the building and the bridge failure lacked believable physics. Kimi K3 landed somewhere in between.

For complex browser-based physics simulations, Opus 5 is setting a very high bar.

items.title: Opus 5 vs Kimi K3 vs GPT-5.6 vs Claude Fable 5; This is actually wild.
items.summary:
Opus 5 vs Kimi K3 vs GPT-5.6 vs Claude Fable 5; This is actually wild.

Someone ran Claude Fable 5 and Kimi K3 side by side on the same prompt, with the same task, in a single shot.

Both completed it successfully on the first attempt.

The surprise was the cost.

Fable 5: $37.94
Kimi K3: $16.45

That’s a much smaller gap in capability than many people expected, especially for long-running reasoning tasks.

If these results hold up across more benchmarks, AI development workflows could get a lot cheaper.

The setup only works for a limited time, so if you’re planning to try it, save the guide before it’s gone.

items.title: EVERYONE IS TALKING ABOUT CLAUDE OPUS 5 BUILDING AAA GAMES. ALMOST NOBODY KNOWS WHY
items.summary:
EVERYONE IS TALKING ABOUT CLAUDE OPUS 5 BUILDING AAA GAMES. ALMOST NOBODY KNOWS WHY

Someone asked Claude Opus 5 to build a game inspired by For Honor x Rainbow Six.

Minutes later, it was already generating a playable 3D prototype

After comparing it with GPT-5.6 and other models, the creator called Opus 5 the best AI model for frontend and 3D development he's ever used.

But the real story isn't the game.

It's how Anthropic changed prompting.

Most people still write prompts as if they're talking to GPT-4-era models: long instructions, endless checklists, "verify your answer," "think step by step."

Opus 5 was built differently.

Anthropic's own guide says to stop micromanaging the model. Give it the goal, explain the context, remove unnecessary instructions, and let it reason on its own.

That's why you're suddenly seeing people build games, apps, and production-ready UIs instead of just getting better chat responses.

The biggest Opus 5 upgrade isn't higher benchmark scores.

It's that ai is starting to think like an engineer, not just respond like a chatbot

items.title: The most important person in AI just resurfaced. And NVIDIA wrote him a $5 billion check.
items.summary:
The most important person in AI just resurfaced. And NVIDIA wrote him a $5 billion check.

Ilya Sutskever built the research behind GPT. Co-founded OpenAI. Was Chief Scientist for nearly a decade. If you use any AI model today, his fingerprints are on the foundations.

Then he tried to fire Sam Altman, the whole world watched, and Ilya vanished. Two years of silence.

During that silence he started Safe Superintelligence. No app. No API. No customers. One mission: build safe superintelligence. Nothing else. Raised $3 billion while barely saying a word publicly.

Today NVIDIA put $5 billion into SSI and gave them access to their next-gen Vera Rubin chips. 10x more compute overnight.

Jensen doesn't write checks like that on faith. He asked to see the research first. SSI opened the door. Jensen looked. And bet five billion.

Nobody outside knows exactly what Ilya is building. But the few times he's spoken publicly, he's been remarkably specific about what's wrong with current AI and what he thinks is missing.

His argument: every model today learns during training and then freezes. Like a student who studies for years, takes the exam, and never learns anything new again. Brilliant on the test. Strangely fragile in real life.

Ilya doesn't want smarter models. He wants models that keep learning from experience after you deploy them.

His description of the goal: "I produce a superintelligent 15-year-old. They don't know very much at all. Very eager. You go and be a programmer, you go and be a doctor, go and learn."

Not an AI that already knows everything. An AI that can learn anything.

He also talked about something that I haven't stopped thinking about. He said humans have an internal compass — emotions, intuition, gut feel — that tells you something is going wrong long before you reach the end. You don't finish a 10,000-step project and then realize it was broken. You feel it midway.

He said AI needs the same mechanism. Some kind of internal judgment that runs while the model is working. And then said there's a "missing machine learning principle" he can't discuss publicly.

Everyone else is racing to make models bigger. More data. More tokens. More compute.

Ilya is trying to solve something different. How to make them actually learn.

The man who sees more AI research than anyone alive just bet $5 billion that Ilya found it.

items.title: OPENAI IS SO WORRIED THEY HAVE PAUSED TRAINING
items.summary:
OPENAI IS SO WORRIED THEY HAVE PAUSED TRAINING

“This is the first security incident that I have felt very viscerally. I've been a little surprised that more people don't feel it so viscerally.

We paused training. We have to figure out how to secure our sandboxing in a world of multiple zero days being chained together.

We may have to pace the rate of AI development to give ourselves enough time for society to harden around these new capability levels."

items.title: Sam Altman, CEO of OpenAI:
items.summary:
Sam Altman, CEO of OpenAI: 

"It figured out that it could basically cheat on the test by chaining together multiple zero-day exploits to break out of the sandbox, get access to the internet, and then break through multiple systems on the Hugging Face side to get the answer to the test and look really good on the eval."

That was an unreleased model. Nobody asked it to hack anything. They asked it to score well.

They paused training.

It was not trying to escape. It was trying to pass. Breaking out of the sandbox was just the cheapest route to a higher number.

We keep testing these systems for whether they want to hurt us. This one just wanted a good grade.

items.title: SAM ALTMAN CALLED OPENAI A "COMPANY" TO ELON MUSK'S FACE IN 2015.
items.summary:
SAM ALTMAN CALLED OPENAI A "COMPANY" TO ELON MUSK'S FACE IN 2015.

Elon stopped him cold.

"OpenAI is structured as a 501(c)3 nonprofit."

Not a company. A nonprofit. Built specifically so no one would ever profit from it.

Sam nodded.

Then spent the next 10 years running it.

Then converted it into a for-profit company valued at $300 billion.

With shareholders.

With investors expecting returns.

The correction Elon gave him in that interview was not a small vocabulary note.

It was the entire point of OpenAI's existence.

The nonprofit structure was not a legal technicality.

It was the promise.

The thing that made it different from every other AI lab racing to make money.

Sam knew that in 2015.

He was corrected on it by the co-founder in real time.

And then he changed the structure anyway.

The interview exists.

The correction is on tape.

The conversion happened.

@elonmusk
 is in court arguing this exact point right now.

The evidence is the 2015 interview.

Screenshot this.

Follow @cyrilXBT for every OpenAI development the mainstream refuses to connect the dots on.

items.title: Sam on being a parent while running OpenAI:
items.summary:
Sam on being a parent while running OpenAI:

“I think I have the best, most interesting job in the world, and it is still a very distant second to having kids.”

“My kids will never grow up in a world where they were smarter than computers.”

“People ask me, now that you have kids, do you care more about AI safety?

The answer is, I didn't need kids for that. I really didn't want to destroy the world before.”

items.title: Sam Altman said the Hugging Face incident was far more terrifying to him than it seemed to be for many others, and that
items.summary:
Sam Altman said the Hugging Face incident was far more terrifying to him than it seemed to be for many others, and that he genuinely does not understand why more people did not react the same way.

The incident was serious enough to pause the model’s training.

He also suggested that new safety and protection mechanisms may need to exist before this technology is released broadly.

That may be a legitimate concern. It may also be fear-driven marketing. Because if OpenAI slows down, weakens GPT-6, or refuses to release a strong version, China will not politely stop advancing.

The difficult part is building real safeguards without turning them into regulatory capture, cartel behavior, or coordination between the largest AI labs to control who gets access to frontier intelligence.

items.title: OpenAI admits its agent went rogue, triggering a major hack
items.summary:
The OpenAI admission was announced after Hugging Face said in a blog post last week that it had been targeted in an AI-led attack that was “different from anything we had handled before.” Hugging Face said its own AI had been integral to detecting and investigating the breach. [...] In its own post on Tuesday, OpenAI said that it had discovered its agent was behind the attack “after investigating.” The agent was driven by models that included GPT-5.6 Sol and another unreleased, unnamed model. OpenAI said it would work with Hugging Face to further investigate the incident.

“We consider this incident to be an unprecedented cyber incident, involving state-of-the-art cyber capabilities, and are responding accordingly,” OpenAI wrote. [...] OpenAI said in its post that it would also add more protections to its training environments. “This incident points to the need to further strengthen our model’s alignment, cyber protections during evaluation time, and monitoring during internal testing,” the company wrote.

Torr says some companies may not have been as forthcoming as OpenAI and Hugging Face, adding that independent AI safety research is increasingly crucial as time goes on.
